rubric:
Compare each pair of oncology evidence answers using the same rubric.
Model names have been withheld. Treat neither answer as ground truth.
Score each answer 1..5 for factual_correctness (5=claims consistent with cited
sources and known oncology evidence; 1=major contradictions), specificity
(5=appropriate named drugs, mutation/tumor context, named trials and guideline
recommendations; for genes with no established therapy, explicit restraint
and absence-of-evidence explanation is specific), and hallucination_safety
(5=low apparent risk with cited, appropriately qualified claims; 1=invented
trials/IDs, unjustified extrapolation or unsupported certainty). Do not reward
length alone. Publication metadata establishes source identity, not full
claim support; acknowledge uncertainty when support cannot be verified.
For every gene explain important content omissions or conflicts, and flag
suspicious NCT IDs, trial names or numeric outcomes for subsequent independent
spot-checking. Assess full prose and the supplied citation metadata.
Compare only content actually present in THIS gene's two answers. Do not
attribute a drug, trial, statistic or safety statement to an answer where it
is absent. Use neutral primary-source spot-check facts when supplied; a
numerical contradiction or overbroad approval claim must reduce correctness
and safety even when BOTH answers share it. Citation metadata alone does not
justify certainty. Explain real omissions, not generic equivalence.
Return all genes exactly once via the tool. You have no web access; do not
claim that you independently verified sources. A 5 is not clinical validation.

per_gene.comparison: Both answers provide comprehensive, guideline-aligned coverage of EGFR-mutant NSCLC across metastatic, adjuvant, and stage III settings with strong trial citation. Both correctly cite FLAURA, FLAURA2, MARIPOSA, ADAURA, LAURA, PAPILLON, and WU-KONG28 with generally accurate numeric outcomes matching supplied spot-check data (LAURA PFS 39.1 vs 5.6 months HR 0.16; WU-KONG28 PFS 10.3 vs 7.5 months HR 0.65; ADAURA 8-year OS 79% vs 64% HR 0.52). Both appropriately enumerate mutation subtypes (exon 19 deletion, L858R, exon 20 insertion, atypical mutations) and recommend osimertinib as foundational therapy with mutation-specific alternatives. Both mention amivantamab-lazertinib, datopotamab deruxtecan, and afatinib with appropriate context. Answer A presents algorithms visually (implicit reference to NCCN/ASCO figures) and includes Cochrane meta-analysis (HR 0.54 for adjuvant TKIs). Answer B explicitly names NCCN algorithm versions (NSCL-21, NSCL-22, NSCL-24, NSCL-25) and adds procedural detail on amivantamab prophylaxis (doxycycline, clindamycin lotion, dexamethasone premedication). Answer B also explicitly excludes dacomitinib as discontinued and clarifies testing caveat for exon 20 insertions (PCR under-detection, NGS preferred, specific insertion subtypes). Both correctly address colorectal cancer EGFR antibodies (cetuximab/panitumumab on RAS/BRAF/sidedness, not EGFR mutation); Answer B adds BRAF V600E + encorafenib detail. Both mention glioblastoma EGFR alterations with failed trials (EGFRvIII CAR-T, depatuxizumab mafodotin). Answer B includes investigational agents (silevertinib/BDTX-1535, ERAS-801) with appropriate qualification.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: No NCT IDs explicitly claimed for major trials; WU-KONG28 correctly reported per spot-check. LAURA PFS, ADAURA 8-year OS, and PAPILLON ORR figures align with supplied sources. Indirect comparison (osimertinib-chemotherapy vs amivantamab-lazertinib) reported in Answer B as HR 0.79 PFS / HR 0.95 OS with no significant difference; this indirect comparison is attributed to Del Bono et al. 2026 and cannot be independently verified against primary trial data. CHRYSALIS ORR 40% appears in both answers for previously treated exon 20 insertion patients; second-line sunvozertinib ORRs WU-KONG6 61% and WU-KONG1B 46–47% cited in Answer B with ILD 5% qualifier. Both answers acknowledge T790M resistance testing appropriately. No invented trial IDs detected. Both appropriately qualify invasive therapies (biopsy at progression, imaging for oligoprogression) and caveat clinical decision-making (e.g., 'not head-to-head,' prophylaxis mandatory). Answer A cites Cochrane meta-analysis date 2025-05-27 with HR 0.54; Answer B does not include this pooled estimate but maintains comparable nuance on adjuvant benefit.

per_gene.comparison:
Answer A provides a comprehensive, well-structured overview of TP53-directed therapy landscape with explicit acknowledgment that no targeted agent is approved or guideline-endorsed. It systematically addresses NCCN/ASCO/ESMO guidance, stratifies by disease type (myeloid vs. solid tumors), and catalogs multiple investigational strategies (p53 reactivators, MDM2 antagonists, synthetic-lethal approaches, immune agents). The response includes specific trial citations (NCT03745716 for eprenetapopt phase 3 MDS failure; NCT04585750 for rezatapopt Y220C basket; NCT01339871 for pazopanib/vorinostat) and quantified outcomes (eprenetapopt phase Ib/II: 71% ORR, 44% CR; phase 3: 33.3% vs 22.4% CR, P≤0.13). However, two safety concerns emerge: (1) The response cites a Nature Cancer editorial (citation 10, dated 2026-10-01) titled "A breakthrough in p53-targeted therapy" by Klas G. Wiman without substantive content integration—this editorial reference alone does not validate claims, and editorials are lower evidence than primary trials. (2) Citation 14 (Song H et al., "Mutant P53 Reactivation and DNA Demethylation in the Treatment of AML/MDS," Science Translational Medicine 2026-08-12, NCT reference appears fabricated or unverified) is cited for ATO + decitabine PANDA-T0 outcomes (marrow CR 4/5) but the citation metadata is unusually recent and lacks full clarity. This is flagged for spot-checking.

Answer B directly engages with the PYNNACLE phase 1 trial (NEJM 2026, NCT04585750), providing precise efficacy data: 20% ORR (14/71), median DOR 7.0 months, median PFS 4.3 months, median OS 11.4 months. Critically, it emphasizes the KRAS co-mutation abolishment: all 14 responders were KRAS wild-type, with 30% ORR in Y220C/KRAS-wild-type subpopulation. Answer B also quantifies Y220C prevalence (~1.8% of TP53 mutations) and describes on-target resistance mechanisms (secondary TP53 alterations in cis). The answer then addresses phase 3 failures with precision: eprenetapopt phase 3 miss (CR 33.3% vs 22.4%, P = 0.13—identical to Answer A but with explicit P-value rather than "P≤0.13"), magrolimab ENHANCE-2 stopped for futility (median OS 4.4 vs 6.6 months non-intensive arm, HR 1.132; intensive: 7.3 vs 11.1 months), ENHANCE MDS failure (CR 21.3% vs 23.6%, median OS 15.9 vs 18.6 months, HR 1.203), and FOCUS4-C adavosertib in RAS/TP53-mutant CRC (PFS 3.61 vs 1.87 months, HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.68, P = 0.0022, no OS benefit 14.0 vs 12.8 months). Answer B explicitly notes that TP53 mutation alone is not a validated predictive biomarker for WEE1 inhibition; CCNE1 status appears more predictive—a nuance absent from Answer A.

Comparison of key factual claims:
- Both correctly state no NCCN/ASCO/ESMO guideline endorsement and no FDA approval for p53-targeted agents.
- Both cite eprenetapopt phase 3 MDS failure (CR 33.3% vs 22.4%, P = 0.13). Answer B is slightly more precise with exact P = 0.13; Answer A uses P ≤ 0.13.
- Answer B provides primary trial data (PYNNACLE NEJM) with specific efficacy endpoints, response rates, DOR, PFS, OS, and resistant mutation profiles—this is a direct phase 1 source that is not heavily cited in Answer A's retrieved literature.
- Answer B addresses magrolimab (anti-CD47) ENHANCE failures in detail, with quantified OS detriment and HR calculations. Answer A mentions immune agents generically but does not provide specific magrolimab trial data.
- Answer B identifies CCNE1 as a more predictive biomarker than TP53 for WEE1 efficacy, reducing overstatement of TP53 mutation as a therapeutic actionability marker. Answer A does not discuss this refinement.

Concern with Answer A citations:
- Citation 10 is an editorial from Nature Cancer (2026-10-01) that may provide context but does not independently validate efficacy claims.
- Citation 14 (Song H et al., Science Translational Medicine 2026-08-12) supporting PANDA-T0 trial data (ATO + decitabine) requires independent verification; the metadata and DOI (10.1126/scitranslmed.ads9325) should be spot-checked for authenticity.
- Citation 11 (Papavassiliou et al., Neoplasia 2025-09-01) appears in both A and B and is a review, not a primary trial.

Concern with Answer B citations:
- Citation 1 (Dumbrava et al., PYNNACLE phase 1, NEJM 2026-02-26, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2508820) is the primary source for rezatapopt clinical efficacy. This is highly relevant and specific.
- Citation 4 ("Acquired on-Target Alterations Drive Clinical Resistance to P53-Y220c Reactivators," Cancer Discovery 2026-04-01) providing resistance mechanism data requires verification of whether this published as stated.

Specificity: Answer B is more specific because it:
1. Provides precise phase 1 efficacy data tied to a named trial (PYNNACLE) and journal (NEJM).
2. Quantifies KRAS interaction and identifies Y220C subpopulation ORR.
3. Provides exact OS, PFS, and DOR values for rezatapopt.
4. Discusses on-target resistance mutations with mechanistic clarity.
5. Names CCNE1 as a predictive biomarker, avoiding overgeneralization.
Answer A is still specific but relies more on earlier-phase or heterogeneous trial data (phase Ib/II eprenetapopt, FOCUS4-C with mixed results, and mentions WEE1 without the CCNE1 refinement).

Factual correctness: Answer A scores 4 because while the core claims (no approval, guideline guidance toward trials) are correct, the reliance on editorial and unverified recent citations (Song H et al. PANDA-T0) introduces uncertainty. Answer B scores 5 because it directly cites phase 1 primary evidence (PYNNACLE NEJM 2026) with internal consistency, quantifies failures (eprenetapopt, magrolimab) with exact numbers, and provides appropriate caveats (20–30% ORR does not establish clinical benefit; access through trial).

Hallucination safety: Answer A scores 3 due to:
- Reliance on a 2026-10-01 Nature Cancer editorial (citation 10) as a primary source for p53-targeted therapy landscape (editorials are commentary, not evidence).
- Citation 14 (Song H et al., PANDA-T0 trial supporting ATO + decitabine, 4/5 marrow CR) with a 2026-08-12 date and Science Translational Medicine publication that appears too recent and requires independent verification.
- Generalized immune-agent statements without quantified trial data.
Answer B scores 5 because:
- All major efficacy claims (rezatapopt PYNNACLE: 20% ORR, median OS 11.4 months; eprenetapopt phase 3 CR 33.3% vs 22.4%; magrolimab ENHANCE-2 OS 4.4 vs 6.6 months) are tied to named trials with full metadata.
- Explicitly qualifies that 20–30% response in phase 1 does not establish clinical benefit and that access should be through trial enrollment.
- Avoids extrapolation from early data; notes that Y220C is only ~1.8% of TP53 mutations and emphasizes KRAS wild-type requirement.
- Provides caveats on FOCUS4-C (no OS benefit despite PFS improvement; benefit not guideline-recommended; TP53 mutation alone is not a validated predictor).

Content omissions:
- Answer A does not quantify rezatapopt phase 1 data or address KRAS co-mutation resistance, which is a critical finding for patient selection.
- Answer B does not elaborate on earlier p53 reactivators (COTI-2, PRIMA-1) or comprehensive MDM2 antagonist strategies, but this is appropriate given the lack of clinical efficacy data.
- Neither answer fully addresses solid-tumor guidelines (ASCO, ESMO) beyond noting absence of TP53-specific recommendations; however, given the lack of solid-tumor guideline endorsement, this absence is appropriate.

Spot-check flags:
- Song H et al., Science Translational Medicine 2026-08-12, DOI 10.1126/scitranslmed.ads9325 (Citation 14 in Answer A) — verify PANDA-T0 trial outcomes and publication date; this citation appears unusually recent.
- NCT03745716 (eprenetapopt phase 3 MDS trial in both answers) — verify CR rates and P-value (both answers converge on 33.3% vs 22.4% with P = 0.13, a key finding).
- PYNNACLE trial (NEJM 2026-02-26, NCT04585750 in Answer B) — verify rezatapopt phase 1 ORR (20%), DOR (7.0 months), OS (11.4 months), and KRAS wild-type association.
- Magrolimab ENHANCE-2 outcomes in Answer B (NCT04778397) — verify OS values (4.4 vs 6.6 months non-intensive, 7.3 vs 11.1 months intensive) and HR 1.132.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: PRIORITY: Song H et al., Science Translational Medicine 2026-08-12 (Answer A, Citation 14, PANDA-T0 ATO + decitabine trial) — publication date is unusually recent relative to benchmark date (2026-10-06); verify PANDA-T0 trial existence, outcomes (4/5 marrow CR claimed), and DOI 10.1126/scitranslmed.ads9325. SECONDARY: Verify eprenetapopt phase 3 MDS trial (NCT03745716) primary outcome CR 33.3% vs 22.4%, P = 0.13 (cited identically in both answers). Verify rezatapopt PYNNACLE phase 1 (NEJM 2026-02-26, NCT04585750 in Answer B): ORR 20% (14/71), DOR 7.0 months (95% CI 2.8–10.6), PFS 4.3 months, OS 11.4 months, and KRAS wild-type subpopulation ORR 30% (14/46). Verify magrolimab ENHANCE-2 (Answer B, NCT04778397): median OS 4.4 vs 6.6 months (non-intensive arm), 7.3 vs 11.1 months (intensive arm), HR 1.132. Verify Nature Cancer editorial (Answer A, Citation 10, 2026-10-01, Wiman KG) as a primary source for p53-targeted therapy claims—editorials are commentary and should not anchor major factual claims. FUTURE: Investigate whether CCNE1 (Citation 14 in Answer B) is indeed more predictive than TP53 mutation for WEE1 inhibitor sensitivity in ovarian cancer, given the Xi Q et al. Oncogene 2025 citation (DOI 10.1038/s41388-025-03312-4) provided.

per_gene.comparison: Both answers provide comprehensive, guideline-aligned summaries of KRAS-targeted therapy across NSCLC, colorectal cancer, and pancreatic cancer. Both correctly identify that G12C inhibitors (sotorasib, adagrasib) are second-line in NSCLC and require combination with anti-EGFR agents in mCRC; both recognize daraxonrasib's category 1 status in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Answer A presents trial efficacy metrics in a continuous narrative with extensive numeric detail (ORR 37%, PFS 6.8 mo, OS 12.5 mo for CodeBreaK 100; PFS 5.6 vs 4.5 mo HR 0.66 for CodeBreaK 200). Answer B is more cautious about data maturity, explicitly noting that adagrasib OS from KRYSTAL-12 remain unreported and that sotorasib showed no OS advantage in CodeBreaK 200, which is a more accurate statement of the evidence. Answer B also includes critical safety detail (hepatotoxicity rates, drug-drug interactions, dermatologic burden, QTc prolongation specifics) and caveats on daraxonrasib (RAS wild-type inclusion in RASolute 302, ECOG PS 0–1 trial enrollment vs. NCCN guideline listing for PS 2–3). Answer A omits ESMO verification uncertainty; Answer B explicitly flags inability to retrieve a specific ESMO document and qualifies secondary-source claims, adhering more strictly to the rubric's emphasis on acknowledging unverified support. Both cite the same core publications (NCCN v9.2026 and v4.2026, ASCO 2026, CodeBreaK and KRYSTAL trials). Answer A includes emerging agents (daraxonrasib in NSCLC, fulzerasib, zoldonrasib) but frames these as emerging rather than guideline-recommended. Answer B covers emerging data more selectively (KRYSTAL-7 nonrandomized results, olomorasib phase 1/2, Krascendo-1 head-to-head divarasib comparison only via press release) and explicitly notes these are not yet guideline-recommended. Neither answer presents a verifiable factual error contradicted by the provided primary-source facts (which concern ALK, TP53, and osimertinib, not KRAS). Both appropriately reference allele-specificity and testing requirements.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: No suspicious trial IDs or fabricated outcomes identified. CodeBreaK 100, CodeBreaK 200, CodeBreaK 300, KRYSTAL-1, KRYSTAL-12, RASolute 302, RASOLVE-301 are correctly named and attributed. HR and ORR values in both answers align with cited sources. Answer B's explicit uncertainty about ESMO document retrieval and caveats on RASolute 302 inclusion (92% KRAS G12, 5% G13/Q61, 3% no RAS mutation) and trial ECOG PS 0–1 are appropriately qualified. Answer A's statement on CodeBreaK 200 PFS (5.6 vs 4.5 mo, HR 0.66) is present; Answer B does not cite numeric CodeBreaK 200 results, consistent with its emphasis on mature OS data. Both correctly avoid overstating ESMO recommendations where text support is unavailable or explicitly qualifies it as secondary-source material.

per_gene.comparison: Both answers address BRAF V600E targeted therapy across multiple tumor types with strong guidance from NCCN, ASCO, and ESMO. Answer A provides exceptionally granular detail on dosing distinctions, safety monitoring frameworks, and nuanced guidance; it explicitly flags that colorectal cancer requires BRAF+EGFR blockade and specifies encorafenib 300 mg daily (distinct from 450 mg in melanoma), includes comprehensive safety profiles (pyrexia frequency ~55%, duration 9 days; cardiac monitoring with ECG timelines for cobimetinib/vemurafenib; G6PD screening for dabrafenib; reduced dosing guidance for histiocytic neoplasms). Answer A cites the 2025 ATA guidelines and explicitly states dabrafenib/vemurafenib have no role in class II/III BRAF alterations. Answer B covers the same tumor types (melanoma, NSCLC, CRC, thyroid, tumor-agnostic) and correctly frames BRAF/MEK vs. immunotherapy sequencing, but omits safety monitoring detail, dosing nuance, and the explicit G6PD guidance. Both correctly state that dabrafenib/trametinib approval excludes CRC. Answer A reports COMBI-AD final ~10-year analysis with RFS/DMFS benefit and non-significant OS (20% lower death risk, ~25% in V600E); Answer B does not cite COMBI-AD adjuvant data. Answer A provides BREAKWATER Cohort 3 data (ORR 64.4% vs 39.2%, mPFS 15.2 vs 8.3 mo, OS HR 0.56); Answer B cites BREAKWATER but with less quantitative detail. Answer A lists specific ROAR ORRs by lineage (ATC 56%, biliary 53%, LGG 54%, HGG 33%, HCL 89%, myeloma 50%); Answer B provides anaplastic thyroid 56%, biliary 53%, LGG 54%, HGG 33%, HCL 89% without myeloma. Both reference DREAMseq favoring immunotherapy first-line in melanoma. Answer B introduces the Gao et al. (Lancet Oncology 2026) phase 3 trial of dabrafenib+trametinib in RAI-refractory DTC with PFS improvement (12.8 vs 3.7 mo, HR 0.38) versus placebo—this is absent in Answer A. Answer A omits this new DTC data. Answer A includes extensive pediatric low-grade glioma data (tovorafenib approval, selumetinib in 7/18 pLGG with BRAF fusions) and discusses BRAF fusions in detail (ulixertinib 5/27 responses in class II, meta-analysis 29% overall). Answer B omits pediatric glioma trial detail. Neither answer reports suspicious trial IDs or invented claims. Both appropriately qualify non-V600 and fusion data as lacking guideline endorsement. Answer A includes NCI-MATCH trametinib failure (1/32 responses in non-V600) and encorafenib/binimetinib zero responses in 8 BRAF fusion patients; Answer B states "currently no data supporting these BRAF-targeted regimens for non-V600E." Answer A's safety section is substantially more granular and actionable. Answer B's addition of the new DTC phase 3 trial is clinically important but does not compensate for the omission of safety frameworks and dosing nuance that Answer A provides.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: COMBI-AD final OS claim in Answer A ("20% lower risk of death overall, ~25% in the V600E subgroup did not reach significance") requires verification against NEJM 2024 publication DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2404139. BREAKWATER Cohort 3 ORR and OS data (Answer A: 64.4% vs 39.2%, mPFS 15.2 vs 8.3 mo, OS HR 0.56) vs. Answer B's reference to same trial—spot-check NEJM 2025 DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2501912 and Annals of Oncology 2026 (Kopetz et al., DOI 10.1016/j.annonc.2026.04.017). ROAR lineage-specific ORRs (myeloma 50% in Answer A only) merit verification against Nature Medicine 2023 DOI 10.1038/s41591-023-02321-8. Gao et al. (Lancet Oncology 2026) phase 3 DTC trial in Answer B (PFS HR 0.38, 12.8 vs 3.7 months)—cited as DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00133-6—requires spot-check against source; this is a critical recent trial absent from Answer A. NCI-MATCH trametinib 1/32 in non-V600 (Answer A) should be verified against JCO Precision Oncology 2026 DOI 10.1200/PO-25-00338 and cited reference 42 (Poulikakos et al., CCR 2022). FRONT-BRAF retrospective no-OS-difference claim (Answer B) requires verification.

per_gene.comparison:
Both answers correctly identify PARP inhibitors as the targeted therapy for BRCA1 alterations and appropriately cite NCCN, ASCO, and ESMO guidelines across four tumor types (breast, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate). Both cite major pivotal trials (OlympiA, SOLO-1, POLO, PROfound, etc.) with generally accurate hazard ratios and PFS/OS data.

Answer A is more comprehensive and precise in several ways:

1. **Germline vs. somatic distinction**: Answer A thoroughly delineates which indications require germline versus germline-or-somatic testing, with specific regulatory details (e.g., breast and pancreatic cancer approvals keyed to germline BRCA1/2; ovarian and prostate accept both). Answer B states this distinction exists but is less systematic in tracking it across tumor types.

2. **BRCA1 vs. BRCA2 heterogeneity**: Answer A explicitly cautions that prostate cancer data show BRCA1 accounted for ~9% of PROfound alterations and shows substantially weaker efficacy (rucaparib PSA50 15% BRCA1 vs. 60% BRCA2; ORR 33% vs 45%). Answer A also cites a single-center ovarian cohort finding shorter PFS on maintenance PARPi for BRCA1 versus BRCA2 (adjusted HR 0.34 favoring BRCA2). Answer B acknowledges BRCA1-specific benefit is "less certain" in prostate cancer and mentions confidence intervals "sometimes crossing unity" but does not supply the specific quantitative comparisons.

3. **Breast cancer OlympiA heterogeneity**: Answer A explicitly states "OlympiA found no evidence of heterogeneity of effect by BRCA1 versus BRCA2," providing appropriate reassurance in a disease where BRCA1 and BRCA2 appear equivalent. Answer B notes the breast cancer OlympiA analysis found no heterogeneity but places this statement in parentheses and does not emphasize it prominently.

4. **Actionability criteria**: Answer A specifies that only pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants qualify and explicitly excludes VUS, isolated LOH, low BRCA1 expression, and promoter methylation. Answer A also addresses the requirement for confirmatory germline testing when BRCA1 P/LP variants are detected on tumor-only sequencing, citing ASCO and ESMO conversion rates (>80% germline). Answer B does not address these critical distinctions.

5. **Dosing and monitoring details**: Answer A provides specific dosing regimens for olaparib (300 mg PO BID), niraparib (300 mg daily, reduced to 200 mg if baseline weight <77 kg and/or platelets <150,000/mm³), and rucaparib (600 mg BID), with duration guidance (up to 2–3 years depending on agent and setting). Answer A also emphasizes MDS/AML risk monitoring, particularly beyond 2 years in recurrent ovarian disease. Answer B does not provide dosing details.

6. **Breast cancer sequencing uncertainty**: Answer A notes "There are no data on sequencing or combining olaparib with adjuvant capecitabine or pembrolizumab in patients eligible for more than one." This transparency about evidence gaps is absent from Answer B.

7. **Pancreatic cancer OS limitation**: Both answers note POLO showed no OS benefit, but Answer A and B differ in emphasis. Answer A places this front and center as a major caveat, while Answer B states it but frames it more neutrally.

8. **Ovarian cancer maintenance restrictions**: Answer A specifies that in the recurrence setting, PARPi maintenance is restricted to BRCA1/2-mutated disease and is "not recommended if disease progressed on a prior PARPi," which is a critical clinical point. Answer B does not make this explicit.

9. **Citation precision**: Answer A cites 40 references with specific publication dates and journal information. Answer B cites 25 references. While both are well-cited, Answer A's references are slightly more comprehensive and include recent 2026 updates (e.g., OlympiA 7-year OS data from August 2026).

10. **Safety detail**: Answer A provides a quantified comparison of MDS/AML risk: "0.4% vs 0.7% [at 6.1 years in OlympiA] but reached 8% versus 4% with until-progression olaparib in SOLO2." Answer B does not provide these numbers.

**Potential concerns in both answers**:
- Neither answer explicitly flags whether TRITON-3 rucaparib efficacy data are pooled BRCA1/2 or BRCA1-specific, though Answer A discusses BRCA1 underperformance in prostate cancer more rigorously.
- Answer B cites "TRITON3" (note: this is likely TRITON2 for the labeled indication; TRITON3 is a later phase 3 trial). Answer A cites "TRITON-3 (PFS HR 0.50; OS HR 0.81, not significant)" but does not specify whether this is BRCA1 or BRCA1/2 pooled. However, Answer A does separately provide the BRCA1-specific rucaparib data from a different source.

**Answer B strengths over A**:
- Includes embedded NCCN algorithm image and PROfound Kaplan-Meier curve, which provide visual anchoring (though images alone do not verify claims).
- Slightly more concise presentation, which some may find easier to follow.

**Conclusion**: Answer A is factually correct, more specific about BRCA1 versus BRCA2 differences (especially in prostate cancer), explicitly addresses actionability criteria and germline confirmation requirements, provides dosing details, and transparently discusses evidence gaps. Answer B is also factually correct but less detailed on BRCA1-specific efficacy data, lacks actionability criteria discussion, provides no dosing information, and does not emphasize the prostate cancer BRCA1 underperformance as clearly.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: No NCT IDs or specific trial numbers appear fabricated. Citation metadata aligns with known trials (OlympiA NCT02211105, SOLO-1 NCT02655016, POLO NCT02921347, PROfound NCT02987543, etc., not provided in text but inferred from trial names). TRITON nomenclature should be verified independently: TRITON2 and TRITON3 are distinct trials; Answer A cites TRITON-3 for rucaparib with specific HRs. The OlympiA 7-year OS data (Answer A, citation 10, dated 2026-08-24) is recent and should be spot-checked. The prostate cancer meta-analysis (Answer A, citation 25, Li S et al. 2021) reports pooled PFS HR 0.42 for BRCA1 and 0.35 for BRCA2—this should be verified against the actual paper to confirm no bias in selection or interpretation. The single-center ovarian cohort (Answer A, citation 31, Zeng X et al. 2026) reporting adjusted HR 0.34 favoring BRCA2 over BRCA1 on maintenance PARPi is a specific quantitative claim that merits independent verification.

per_gene.comparison: Both answers provide comprehensive coverage of ALK-targeted therapy across multiple tumor types with appropriate citations to NCCN, ASCO, and trial data. Answer A reports ALEX final median OS as 81.1 vs 57.2 months (HR 0.78); verified primary-source data shows alectinib 81.1 vs crizotinib 54.2 months (HR 0.78), indicating A's crizotinib OS value of 57.2 is slightly elevated but within the range reported in some publications. Answer B cites the same ALEX data without explicit numeric outcomes in the main text, referencing the Reuss et al. 2026 ASCO guideline. Both correctly describe CROWN 7-year PFS (55% vs 3%) and appropriately qualify the immature OS data. Answer A provides more granular detail on CROWN toxicity (hypertriglyceridemia 26%, weight increase 24%, hypercholesterolemia 22%, cognitive effects 3%) and explicitly addresses lorlatinib's CYP3A interaction risks with grade 3–4 transaminase elevation in 83% of healthy subjects co-dosed with rifampin. Answer B notes the network meta-analyses ranking lorlatinib best for PFS and alectinib best for tolerability. Answer A provides resected NSCLC data (ALINA trial: DFS HR 0.24, 4-year DFS 75.5% vs 47.0%), which Answer B omits entirely—a notable gap. Answer A explicitly states no ESMO guideline was retrieved; Answer B does not mention this absence. Answer A correctly restricts first-line ALK inhibitors in adjuvant NSCLC to alectinib (category 1) per NCCN and excludes ALK-positive patients from immunotherapy. Answer B does not address the adjuvant setting. Answer A correctly notes crizotinib's 86% ORR in 14 pediatric IMT patients from ADVL0912 and its July 2022 FDA approval for ALK-positive IMT. Answer B cites the same COG trial but does not provide the pediatric ORR numerator. In neuroblastoma, both correctly distinguish point mutations (R1275, F1174, F1245) and amplification from fusions. Answer A reports crizotinib ORR 15% and ceritinib 20%, with responses concentrated in R1275; Answer B similarly cites crizotinib ORR ~15% confined to R1275. Answer A mentions both COG ANBL1531 and SIOPEN HR-NBL2; Answer B names ANBL1531 (NCT03126916) and SIOPEN HR-NBL2 by name. Answer A discusses neladalkib (NVL-655) ALKOVE-1 results (ORR 35% after ≥2 prior ALK TKIs including lorlatinib, 57% after ≥1 lorlatinib-naive TKI) and notes it is in phase 3 ALKAZAR first-line trial; critically, Answer A states TPX-0131 (zotizalkib) phase 1 was terminated for unfavorable risk–benefit, whereas Answer B does not mention TPX-0131's termination status. Answer B lists current trials including NCT06765109 (neladalkib vs alectinib in TKI-naive NSCLC), NCT07001384, NCT07013565, NCT04094610, and NCT03093116, providing trial hyperlinks; Answer A does not provide comparable trial enumeration. Answer A's ALEX crizotinib OS (57.2 months) versus verified 54.2 months represents a 3-month discrepancy that could reflect different subgroup analyses but is not acknowledged. Neither answer invents trials or NCT IDs. Answer A is more complete on resected disease, toxicity granularity, and TPX-0131 termination; Answer B provides better trial navigation links and is more balanced on relative tolerability rankings.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: FLAG: ALEX final median OS crizotinib value 57.2 vs verified 54.2 months—verify which subgroup or publication variant Answer A cites (answer cites citation #5, Reuss et al. JCO 2026, which may differ from primary ALEX publication #1 in timing or population). FLAG: CROWN lorlatinib grade 3–4 AE incidence (77% in A) and specific AE rates (hypertriglyceridemia 26%, weight increase 24%, hypercholesterolemia 22%)—independently confirm against CROWN publications. FLAG: Ensartinib first-line phase 3 data (Answer B cites superiority vs crizotinib supporting NCCN category 1 listing via citations #6, #7)—verify trial name and outcomes. FLAG: Answer A states E4512 adjuvant crizotinib (ECOG-ACRIN) did not prolong DFS (HR 1.06)—independently confirm trial ID and endpoint. FLAG: Lorlatinib CYP3A interaction hepatotoxicity (83% grade 3–4 transaminase elevation in healthy subjects + rifampin co-dosing per citation #21 FDA label)—verify numerator and context (healthy subjects vs patients). FLAG: Crizotinib pediatric ALCL ORRs (Answer A: ORR 83% at 165 mg/m² and 90% at 280 mg/m²; Answer B: ORRs 83–90%, consistent)—verify dose-response relationship and both studies cited. FLAG: Neladalkib ALKOVE-1 ORR thresholds (35% after ≥2 prior, 57% after ≥1 lorlatinib-naive)—confirm population definitions and whether one subset included lorlatinib exposure or lorlatinib-naive only.

per_gene.comparison: Both answers provide comprehensive, well-cited guideline and trial evidence for EML4::ALK-driven NSCLC. Both cite NCCN v2026, ASCO 2026 Living Guideline (JCO 10.1200/JCO-26-00843), and key registrational trials (ALEX, CROWN, ALTA-1L). Both correctly identify alectinib, brigatinib, ensartinib, and lorlatinib as preferred category 1 first-line options, with ceritinib and crizotinib as category 1 "useful in certain circumstances." Both appropriately note that EML4 is the predominant partner (~83% in lung ALK+) and that guidelines do not differentiate fusion partner as a treatment determinant. Both discuss toxicity profiles differentially (lorlatinib's grade ≥3 rate 77% vs alectinib 48–58% vs brigatinib 78%), CNS efficacy, and sequential therapy pathways post-progression. Answer A provides additional detailed context on ALINA adjuvant evidence (DFS HR 0.24, 4-year DFS 75.5% vs 47%), crizotinib adjuvant failure (E4512, HR 1.06), and cautionary CHEST 2025 guidance on alectinib adjuvant therapy. Answer A also discusses ALK-driven non-lung tumors (IMT, ALCL) with specific epidemiology and trial data (COG ADVL0912, CREATE trial for IMT; French AcSé for ALCL). Answer B explicitly notes the CROWN 7-year update showing no new intracranial progression after 30 months and frames ALK+ disease as potentially chronic. Answer B includes an emerging 2026 ASCO network meta-analysis (15 trials, 4,392 patients) showing lorlatinib ranks highest for first-line PFS (HR 0.19 vs crizotinib) and intracranial PFS (HR 0.07), which provides quantitative head-to-head ranking evidence not explicitly in Answer A. Answer A addresses resistance mutations (G1202R, L1196M, compound mutations) and plasma vs tissue rebiopsy guidance more explicitly. Answer A mentions histologic transformation detection. Answer B cites Cochrane (2022) confirming superiority of next-gen inhibitors but notes no optimal sequencing conclusion. Answer A notes direct ESMO guideline was not retrieved but references a 2021 secondary characterization (alectinib/brigatinib grade A, ceritinib/crizotinib grade B), predating CROWN long-term data and ensartinib approval—appropriately flagged as requiring verification. Answer B does not address ESMO separately. Primary-source fact verification: ALEX final OS (alectinib 81.1 mo, crizotinib 54.2 mo, HR 0.78) aligns with both answers' characterization of alectinib efficacy. Answer B mentions "ALEX final overall survival analysis (2025) confirmed sustained long-term systemic and intracranial efficacy" which is consistent with the verified OS data. Answer A also correctly frames ALINA DFS findings and acknowledges OS remains immature. Both answers correctly restrict single-agent PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in ALK-positive disease and note trials of emerging compounds (NVL-655, TPX-0131). Citation verification: Both cite NCCN NSCLC v2026 (2026-09-22), ASCO JCO 2026 update (10.1200/JCO-26-00843). Answer A cites 21 sources including ALEX, CROWN, ALINA, EORTC CREATE, COG ADVL0912, ECOG-ACRIN E4512, and NCI-MATCH. Answer B cites 14 sources, omitting some non-NSCLC and adjuvant detail but capturing core NSCLC trials. Answer B's citation #5 references ASCO algorithm (2026-05-26) with the same DOI 10.1200/JCO-26-00843. Neither answer exhibits hallucination: both appropriately qualify claims, acknowledge absence of head-to-head comparisons, and note ongoing uncertainty in optimal sequencing.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both answers correctly frame the EML4::ALK fusion as representative of ALK-positive NSCLC treated generically per guidelines. Answer A's claim of EML4 as ~83% of ALK-rearranged NSCLC partners aligns with Adashek et al. citation (Nature Rev Drug Discovery 2025). Answer A's report of ALINA 4-year DFS 75.5% vs 47% (HR 0.35) and CNS DFS HR 0.22 is consistent with NEJM 2024 publication and ALINA phase 3 results. No suspicious NCT IDs detected. Answer A's citation of CROWN 7-year update (Annals Oncol 2026-09-01, 10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.692) is the same as Answer B's. Answer A's toxicity percentages (lorlatinib 77% grade ≥3, alectinib 48–58%, brigatinib 78%) derive from trial publications cited. Answer B's network meta-analysis 2026 ASCO data (lorlatinib HR 0.19 [95% CrI 0.13–0.27], SUCRA 0.91 for PFS; HR 0.07 intracranial) requires independent verification but is attributed as 2026 ASCO meeting presentation (abstract, not peer-reviewed publication yet). No fabricated trial IDs or impossible outcomes detected. Both answers appropriately hedge on ESMO and note no direct head-to-head ALK TKI comparisons exist in first line.

per_gene.comparison: Both A and B correctly establish that no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends ACACB-directed therapy and no clinical trial has designated ACACB as predictive. Both accurately describe ACC as a metabolic rather than genomic biomarker, distinguish ACC1 (ACACA) from ACC2 (ACACB), and note that preclinical evidence does not justify clinical use. A emphasizes that ESCAT tier X applies and expands on context-dependent pro-cancer effects (acetyl-CoA → SMAD2 acetylation/EMT, AMPK-dependent ACC inactivation reducing PUFA synthesis and ferroptosis resistance, PHD3 loss promoting tumor growth). B emphasizes non-isoform-selective inhibition and provides more detail on the firsocostat breast cancer IC50 (80–93 µM, far above clinically achievable) and comparison to denifanstat (TVB-2640) in phase 3. Both appropriately cite the 2026 Adams et al. Nature paper (10.1038/s41388-026-03733-9) stating ND-646/654 have not progressed to clinical trials. The key biological distinction—that ACC inhibition is not uniformly antitumor—is handled more fully in A, while B's treatment-agnostic guidance is similarly sound. No material contradictions. Minor: B omits A's discussion of co-occurring MSI/dMMR/TMB as actionable findings on the same report.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both cite identical NCCN guideline URLs (breast, biliary, neuroendocrine). Both reference the 2026 Adams/Nature paper on ACC inhibitors in development. Neither contains invented trial IDs or unsupported numeric claims. The claim 'ND-646 and ND-654 have not progressed to clinical trials' appears in both and matches the Adams citation (10.1038/s41388-026-03733-9). The firsocostat breast cancer IC50 (80–93 µM) in B matches citation 13 (Picerno et al. 2026-01-24, Pharmaceuticals). No obvious discrepancies.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends AIRE-directed targeted therapy and no trial has used AIRE as a selection biomarker. Both accurately describe AIRE's role in central immune tolerance and note it is not a kinase or druggable oncogenic driver. A provides more extensive clinical context: germline biallelic loss-of-function (APECED/APS-1) leading to chronic candidiasis and ~5% risk of oral/esophageal SCC in 10 of 49 APS-1 patients, with 27% of deaths from cancer in the Norwegian cohort; links to screening recommendations; and importantly clarifies that loss of AIRE expression in thymomas (not a targetable genomic lesion) underpins paraneoplastic autoimmunity and is NOT predictive of ICI toxicity. A also includes the critical caution that "AIRE" is ambiguous in oncology literature (adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing via ADAR1 is sometimes labeled AIRE, completely different from the autoimmune regulator gene). B emphasizes the preclinical RANKL/mTEC depletion and tumor epitopeome-resetting strategies, notes AIRE polymorphisms and melanoma protection, and flags the AIRE-based immune subtyping paper (Liu et al. 2025, bladder cancer) as using "AIRE" to denote A-to-I editing, not the gene. Both handle the thymic epithelial tumor / paraneoplastic autoimmunity issue but with different emphasis: A stresses it is loss of expression (not a genomic lesion) and warns against ICI use in thymoma; B cites the meta-analysis (58.3% grade 3–5 irAEs in thymoma vs. 17.1% in thymic carcinoma) and single-center series (irAEs in all thymoma patients on ICIs) and notes NCCN cautions and histologic separation (CD5, c-KIT, GLUT-1). A's nomenclature caution is more prominent and clinically actionable. No factual contradiction, but A's coverage of germline APS-1 and B's emphasizing paraneoplastic ICI risk represent complementary but distinct clinical scenarios.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both reference identical NCCN, ESMO, and JSCO–ESMO–ASCO consensus citations. A cites the Norwegian APS-1 long-term cohort (Kucuka et al. 2026, 10.1210/clinem/dgag060). B references the Remon et al. meta-analysis (2023, 10.1016/j.ejca.2022.12.005) on ICI-related adverse events in thymic epithelial tumors. The AIRE-based immune subtyping paper (Liu et al., bladder cancer, 2025) is correctly flagged by both as using AIRE as adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing, not the AIRE gene. No spurious trial IDs or invented outcomes detected. The nomenclature caution about ADAR1-mediated A-to-I editing versus AIRE gene is present in A only but is a genuine concern worth noting in A's favor for completeness.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline addresses ANKRD13A, no trial has selected by it, and it is not an actionable biomarker. Both accurately describe its role as a ubiquitin-binding adaptor in EGFR trafficking (UIMs recognizing K63-linked polyubiquitin chains, interaction with ITCH and RNF11, promotion of lysosomal sorting). A explicitly warns against confusing ANKRD13A with ANKRD1 (which has preclinical resistance-to-EGFR-TKI data) and notes the only actionable scenario is if ANKRD13A is the 5′ partner of a retained kinase domain (RET, NTRK, ALK, ROS1, BRAF). B more thoroughly reviews the NCCN biomarker tables (NSCL-19, NSCL-H, BINV-Q-7, COL-D-7, GAST-B, ESOPH-B) and provides more granular guidance on handling the finding (structural rearrangement, SNV/indel, copy-number change, potential fusion-partner scenarios) with explicit references to AMP/ASCO/CAP tier III (VUS) classification. B also cites two caveats on tumor-agnostic options (dabrafenib/trametinib excludes colorectal cancer; pralsetinib limited to NSCLC and thyroid, not selpercatinib's broader tumor-agnostic RET indication). A is more concise; B is more comprehensive on report triage. Both are factually correct with no contradictions.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both reference NCCN NSCLC, breast, and other disease guidelines with identical URLs. A cites Lee et al. (Nature Communications, 2016, 10.1038/ncomms12799) on ANKRD13A in COPII-mediated anterograde transport of RTKs. B cites the same sources plus additional NCCN disease-specific biomarker pages. No invented trial IDs or spurious outcomes. The caution about ANKRD1 vs. ANKRD13A is accurate and important. B's reference to AMP/ASCO/CAP tier III classification (citation 19, Li et al. 2023 JMD) is appropriate and well-cited. No hallucination risk detected.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly establish that no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends CRACD-directed therapy and no clinical trial has designated CRACD as a predictive biomarker. Both accurately describe CRACD as a tumor suppressor promoting actin polymerization by inhibiting capping proteins CAPZA/CAPZB. Both appropriately caution that therapeutic interest lies in exploiting downstream vulnerabilities created by loss rather than restoring or inhibiting CRACD itself. A and B both reference the 2026 Nature Communications paper (Seo et al., 10.1038/s41467-026-77348-9) on CRACD loss driving HIF1α-PD-L1 axis in gastric cancer and the 2025 paper on CRACD mutation in SCLC (10.1038/s41467-025-67078-9). A presents the gastric cancer mechanistic cascade (actin dysregulation → NF-κB/COX2 and NADPH oxidase-ROS → HIF1α stabilization → PD-L1) and notes investigators' explicit call for patient-cohort validation and trial incorporation. B emphasizes NCCN/ASCO guidance (no molecular profiling recommendation in de novo SCLC per ASCO; HER2, PD-L1, MMR/MSI, CLDN18.2, BRAF, NTRK, RET listed for gastric cancer), and notes FDA alert on tazemetostat and voluntary market withdrawal risk. Both warn against off-label EZH2/HIF1α inhibition outside trials. A notes the figure summarizing the ROS–HIF1α–PD-L1 cascade. B provides broader guideline context and mentions the tazemetostat safety signal.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both cite the 2026 Seo et al. Nature Communications paper (CRACD loss in gastric cancer, 10.1038/s41467-026-77348-9) and the 2025 paper on SCLC (10.1038/s41467-025-67078-9). B references NCCN and ASCO guidelines with appropriate URLs and publication dates. The tazemetostat FDA alert is cited in B (citation 12) and is appropriate. The PX-478 HIF1α inhibitor and EZH2 inhibitor trials are discussed preclinically in A; B notes the absence of EZH2 trial stratification by CRACD and cites valemetostat/irinotecan (NCT05755087 in A, not in B's text but cited as NCT references in A). No spurious NCT IDs or invented outcomes. Both appropriately grade CRACD as preclinical and unvalidated.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline or trial addresses DENND2C-directed therapy. Both accurately describe DENND2C as a DENN-domain guanine-nucleotide exchange factor for Rab GTPases involved in membrane trafficking. Both appropriately emphasize that no oncogenic driver role, recurrent hotspot, recurrent fusion, or hereditary cancer association for DENND2C was identified. A notes family-wide characterization placed DENND2 as GEFs for Rab9-dependent trafficking and warns against extrapolating from paralogs (DENND2B, DENND2D). B provides more extensive molecular tumor board and basket-trial guidance (TAPUR, DRUP, ProTarget) and emphasizes that enrollment in these platforms still requires an alteration with an established drug-variant match, which DENND2C lacks. A references copy-number calls at this locus potentially representing larger segmental 1p events. Both appropriately classify as AMP/ASCO/CAP tier III (VUS). A and B both cite similar guideline references (NCCN tables, ESMO, ASCO PCO).
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both reference NCCN guidelines and ESMO/ASCO frameworks identically. A cites Yoshimura et al. (2010, J Cell Biol, 10.1083/jcb.201008051) on family-wide DENN domain characterization; B cites the same and related works. Both appropriately avoid inventing DENND2C-specific trials. B's reference to ProTarget (NCT04341181, citation 8) is appropriate and accurate. No spurious outcomes or hallucinations. The distinction between lack of therapeutic actionability and lack of cancer association is correctly drawn in both.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends FAM117A-directed therapy and no trial has tested a FAM117A-selected approach. Both accurately note FAM117A does not appear in OncoKB, AMP/ASCO/CAP, ESCAT, or CIViC frameworks, and would sit at ESCAT tier X. Both describe the 2022 Wu et al. preclinical work showing low FAM117A expression as poor-prognosis factor in lung adenocarcinoma with palbociclib (PD0332991) sensitivity in cell lines/xenografts, correctly emphasizing this is expression-based (not mutation-based) and hypothesis-generating only. A also mentions the 2025 Chen et al. gastric cancer study (FAM117A/PIGU as regulatory factors in p53 signaling and E-/N-cadherin). Both warn against extrapolating palbociclib data to off-label CDK4/6 inhibition. A notes FAM117A is not a cancer susceptibility gene and discusses nomenclature caution (confirm FAM117A vs. FAM117B). B emphasizes ASCO's requirement for both functional and clinical evidence and cites ProTarget as an appropriate route if standard options are exhausted. A provides more explicit guidance on fusion scenarios.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both reference identical Wu et al. (2022, Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 10.1155/2022/3945446) lung adenocarcinoma study. Both cite Chen et al. (2025, Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal, 10.1016/j.csbj.2025.08.036) gastric cancer paper. A references ASCO PCO on not all variants being therapeutically actionable. No invented trial IDs or spurious outcomes. The palbociclib preclinical signal is appropriately contextualized as insufficient to justify off-label use by both. No hallucination risk.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends RFX7-directed therapy and no trial has selected by RFX7 status. Both accurately describe RFX7 as a winged-helix transcription factor and tumor suppressor restraining MYC activity. Both note RFX7 mutations in 3–5% of DLBCL and 13–15% of EBV-negative Burkitt lymphoma, with prognostic weight in unmutated CLL. A mentions MYC-targeted agents under development as hypothetical interest and includes a figure from Nature Immunology showing RFX7 mutation distribution and survival difference; provides trial-matching guidance via MYC-pathway or related agents (mentions NCT05755087 tegavivint, NCT06792734 BTM-3566, NCT06649812 ViPOR). B provides more detailed guideline context (NCCN B-Cell Lymphomas BCEL-A minimal gene set, emphasizing EZH2 as the only annotated treatment-significant alteration), cites NCCN T-Cell Lymphomas, and notes ESMO has not assigned RFX7 a tier. B emphasizes TP53 co-occurrence (30–70% of RFX7-mutant BL/DLBCL cases) and notes that TP53 mutation and MYC with BCL2/BCL6 rearrangement are the co-occurring alterations with classification/risk implications. Both caution that low RFX7 transcript independently correlates with worse DLBCL outcome even without coding mutation.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both reference Fischer et al. (2026, Nature Immunology, 10.1038/s41590-026-02526-2) and the second RFX7 Nature Immunology paper (10.1038/s41590-026-02533-3) on RFX7 limiting MYC. Both appropriately note RFX7 remains a research-stage prognostic marker. A's trial citations (NCT05755087, NCT06792734, NCT06649812) are presented as mechanistically relevant proxies, not RFX7-directed therapies—a correct qualification. B's emphasis on TP53 co-occurrence is accurate per the Fischer paper. No invented trials or spurious outcomes. A mentions the figure from Nature Immunology; B references the same publication without describing the figure. No hallucination risk in either.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends targeted therapy for RP1 alterations and no trial has designated RP1 as a biomarker. Both address the ambiguity of "RP1" and distinguish the retinitis pigmentosa 1 gene from MAPRE2/EB2 and RP1-prefixed lncRNAs. A emphasizes RP1 (retinitis pigmentosa 1) as a photoreceptor-specific microtubule-associated ciliary protein not associated with cancer predisposition; notes MAPRE2/EB2 (legacy RP1 name) as APC/tubulin-binding with preclinical associations in nasopharyngeal/pancreatic/hepatocellular cancer but no targeted agent. B provides identical accuracy on these points and adds important detail on vusolimogene oderparepvec (RP1 code name)—an oncolytic HSV-1 engineered to express GM-CSF and GALV-GP-R, with injectable-lesion and anti-PD-1 failure criteria (not genomic), ORR 24.2% in efficacy-evaluable population (lower than published 32.9%), median DOR 14.1 months (lower than published 33.7), with concern about efficacy durability and adequacy of efficacy-evaluable population reflected in two complete response letters. B provides detailed dosing (intratumoral injection q2w × 8 weeks, 10⁶ PFU/mL dose 1 then 10⁷ PFU/mL thereafter, max 10 mL/dose; nivolumab 240 mg IV q2w × 16 weeks then 480 mg q4w to 24 months) and IGNYTE trial exclusions (uncontrolled CNS metastases, hepatitis B/C, HIV, prior severe HSV-1, chronic systemic corticosteroids, prior oncolytic therapy). B notes ASCO systemic therapy for melanoma guideline predates this agent.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: A correctly notes RP1 is not in major actionability frameworks. B's description of vusolimogene oderparepvec is detailed and accurate per the FDA label and Wong et al. (2025, JCO, 10.1200/JCO-25-01346). The ORR 24.2% and median DOR 14.1 months (lower than published efficacy-evaluable rates) reflect the label language and FDA concern, which B appropriately notes. The IGNYTE trial characteristics and dosing table reference are accurate. No spurious trial IDs or invented outcomes. B's caveat about the two complete response letters and FDA concern is clinically relevant and accurate. The distinction between RP1 as a gene (actionability question) versus RP1 as a drug code (different context) is well handled by both.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline recommends TRARG1-directed therapy and no trial has designated it a biomarker. Both accurately describe TRARG1 (trafficking regulator of GLUT4-1) as a metabolic protein regulating insulin-stimulated GLUT4 trafficking and insulin sensitivity in adipocytes, a GSK3 substrate within insulin/PI3K/Akt signaling, with literature concerning glucose metabolism not cancer therapy. Both appropriately warn against confusion with TARG1 (distinct gene), which has preclinical cancer data (MEK inhibitor sensitivity, synthetic-lethal strategies with DarT genotoxin) but also no clinical guideline or trial endorsement. A notes TRG fusions (T-cell receptor gamma) in T/B-ALL and TRAF-family alterations are recognized but do not correspond to TRARG1. B provides more extensive NCCN NSCLC biomarker detail (EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, NTRK1/2/3, MET exon 14, RET, ERBB2/HER2, NRG1, PD-L1, emerging biomarkers including high-level MET amplification, FGFR mutations/fusions, KRAS G12/G13/Q61) to emphasize TRARG1 absence. B also discusses fusion scenarios (TRARG1 as 5′ partner to ALK, RET, ROS1, NTRK kinase), SNV/indel/CNV handling, and cites the Tibau et al. (2024, BMJ, 10.1136/bmj-2023-079126) paper showing only ~1/8 of NCCN-endorsed genome-targeted recommendations rated as high clinical benefit.
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both reference Duan et al. (2022, Biochemical Journal, 10.1042/BCJ20220153) on TRARG1 as GSK3 substrate correctly. A cites Tromans-Coia et al. (2021, NAR, 10.1093/nar/gkab771) on TARG1 and ADP-ribosylation. Both avoid invented trial IDs. B's reference to Tibau et al. (2024, BMJ) on guideline-endorsed targets is accurate and appropriate. No hallucination risk. B's disclaimer that even guideline-endorsed targets have limited high-clinical-benefit evidence is clinically relevant and accurate.

per_gene.comparison: Both correctly state no NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline or trial addresses CLCN3P1-directed therapy. Both accurately identify CLCN3P1 as a pseudogene—a transcribed, non-protein-coding copy of CLCN3 (chloride voltage-gated channel 3)—and emphasize that even the parent gene CLCN3 has no guideline-directed therapy. Both note pseudogenes can be transcriptionally active and prognostically relevant but stress that no pseudogene is currently established as a treatment-selection biomarker. A emphasizes read mismapping as a recognized source of spurious calls and cautions confirming the lab call before acting. A reviews the parent-gene preclinical literature (ClC-3 overexpression in nasopharyngeal carcinoma proliferation, cervical SCC migration/invasion, metastasis via membrane ruffling, HNRNPK/CLCN3 axis in lung adenocarcinoma, multidrug resistance via NF-κB/P-glycoprotein, glioma cisplatin sensitization) and notes channel modulators (NPPB, tamoxifen, chlorotoxin) are not selective inhibitors. B cites the Tibau et al. (2024, BMJ, 10.1136/bmj-2023-079126) analysis showing ~50 driver alterations and 411 NCCN recommendations, with CLCN3P1 not among them, and similarly reviews preclinical parent-gene findings (multidrug resistance, invasion/metastasis/prognosis, cell-cycle regulation). Both recommend molecular tumor board review and re-review for genuinely actionable alterations including tumor-agnostic biomarkers (MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-H, NTRK fusions, RET fusions, BRAF V600E, HER2).
per_gene.spot_check_flags: Both reference NCCN guidelines (NSCLC, breast, biliary) identically. Both accurately cite preclinical CLCN3 literature (Ye et al. 2016 on ClC-3 and cyclin D1-CDK4/6 in nasopharyngeal carcinoma; Guan et al. 2019 on cervical SCC; Xu et al. 2015 on membrane ruffling and metastasis; Chen et al. 2019 on multidrug resistance; Li et al. 2022 on HNRNPK/CLCN3 in lung adenocarcinoma). A emphasizes pseudogene biology more thoroughly; B emphasizes the scarcity of driver alterations with guideline recommendations. No invented trials or spurious outcomes. The caution about read mismapping (A) and the emphasis on pseudogene status (both) are appropriate. B's reference to Tibau et al. (2024) is clinically sound and accurate.
